0.0.n: Combine this with ございます for a polite morning greeting.

0.1.n: ござい is part of ございます; it is not used alone here.

0.2.n: ます completes ございます, making the greeting polite.

0.4.n: This hesitation word helps the speaker begin speaking tentatively.

1.0.n: Without ございます, this greeting sounds casual.

2.0.n: The speaker means the listener’s voice; Japanese leaves whose voice unstated.

2.1.n: が marks 声 as what is being described.

2.2.n: Literally small, this adjective describes low volume when used with 声.

2.3.n: ん is shortened の and frames the observation as something to confirm.

2.4.n: じゃ is a casual shortening of では and combines with ない to make a negative.

2.5.n: ない supplies the negative in じゃない, used here to seek agreement.

2.6.n: の gives the question an explanatory tone before かい.

2.7.n: かい is a familiar question ending, often associated with masculine or older speakers.

3.0.n: This is a stammered start to おはよう, not a separate word.

3.2.n: The speaker repeats the greeting after being challenged about their volume.

3.3.n: ござい is the part of ございます that comes before ます.

3.4.n: ます completes the formal greeting despite the nervous start.

4.0.n: もっと asks for more volume here; the rest of the instruction is omitted.

5.0.n: This greeting is repeated in response to the demand for more volume.

5.1.n: ござい forms ございます together with ます.

5.2.n: ます keeps the repeated greeting polite.

6.0.n: The speaker again demands more volume using this single word.

7.0.n: The greeting is repeated again, now with greater force.

7.1.n: ござい belongs to the fixed polite greeting おはようございます.

7.2.n: ます maintains politeness even when the greeting is shouted.

8.0.n: This reply uses the casual version without ございます.

9.0.n: The particle が is omitted after this noun in casual speech.

9.1.n: Literally big, this adjective describes high volume when paired with 声.

9.4.n: The speaker hesitates before trying to continue the conversation.

10.0.n: あんた is a blunt, familiar form of あなた and can sound rude.

10.1.n: は marks the listener as the topic of the question.

10.2.n: This question word asks for the listener’s identity.

10.3.n: だい adds a familiar, often masculine tone to a question such as 誰だい.

10.5.n: 自己 combines with 紹介 to form the word for introducing yourself.

10.6.n: 紹介 joins 自己 here rather than referring to introducing someone else.

10.7.n: くらい presents introducing yourself as a basic, minimal task.

10.8.n: できんだろ contracts できるんだろう; the ん is not a negative here.

11.0.n: 本日 is a formal alternative to 今日, suitable for workplace introductions.

11.1.n: から marks today as the starting point.

11.2.n: こちら politely points to the company where the speaker is.

11.3.n: の links こちら to 会社, forming a polite way to say this company.

11.4.n: This noun identifies the speaker’s new workplace.

11.5.n: の links the company to its receptionist.

11.6.n: 受付 combines with 嬢 here to name a receptionist role.

11.7.n: 嬢 makes 受付嬢 specifically female; the term can sound dated.

12.0.n: The listener’s voice is the subject, though the owner is unstated.

12.1.n: が marks 声 as what the speaker judges to be quiet.

12.2.n: Small describes voice volume here, and the sharp delivery makes it a complaint.

13.0.n: 本日 gives the introduction a formal workplace tone.

13.1.n: から marks when the new job begins.

13.2.n: こちら refers politely to the company the speaker is joining.

13.3.n: の connects こちら with 会社 to identify this company.

13.4.n: This names the organization where the speaker will work.

13.5.n: の connects the company with the receptionist position.

13.6.n: 受付 is the first part of 受付嬢, the job title used here.

13.7.n: 嬢 specifies a female worker in the compound 受付嬢.

13.8.n: として marks the role in which the speaker will work.

13.9.n: 働かせて is the let-work form of 働く; いただく humbly presents the opportunity as a favor received.

13.10.n: こと turns the preceding action into something that can be described as decided.

13.11.n: に marks the resulting arrangement in ことになる.

13.12.n: なりました is polite past なる; with ことに, it says the job arrangement has been decided.

13.14.n: 上村 is the speaker’s family name, read Kamimura here.

13.15.n: と marks 上村 as the name given with 申します.

13.16.n: 申します is the humble, polite form of 言う, commonly used to introduce yourself.

0.tip: おはようございます is the polite greeting; あの here signals hesitation, not that.

1.tip: Dropping ございます makes the greeting casual.

2.tip: For voices, 小さい means quiet rather than physically small.

3.tip: The isolated お shows a nervous stammer at the beginning of おはよう.

4.tip: もっと alone means louder here because the conversation is about voice volume.

5.tip: The speaker keeps the polite greeting while responding to the demand to speak louder.

6.tip: Japanese can omit the entire instruction when one word makes the intended demand clear.

7.tip: A loud delivery does not change the polite form おはようございます.

8.tip: The casual reply contrasts with the other speaker’s polite greetings.

9.tip: 声大きい omits が; 大きい describes a loud voice.

10.lit: You, who are you? Self-introduction at least you can do, right?
10.tip: できんだろ means you can, right here, not you cannot.

11.lit: From today, this company’s female receptionist…
11.tip: The speaker is interrupted before completing the statement about the new job.

12.tip: 声が小さい is a direct complaint about speaking too quietly.

13.lit: From today, as this company’s female receptionist, being allowed to work has been arranged; I am called Kamimura!
13.tip: ことになりました presents the new job as an arrangement that has been decided.
